title: Psalm 77: Remembering God's Wonders in the Night
summary: Sleepless and troubled, the psalmist cries to God through the night and cannot be comforted. He asks whether God has rejected his people forever and whether his loving devotion is gone. Then he resolves to remember the LORD's works of old and recalls the exodus, when God led his people through the sea on a path whose footprints no one could see.
story: Psalm 77 continues the struggle of Book III with God's apparent absence. Psalm 73 wrestled with the prosperity of the wicked, Psalm 74 with the ruined sanctuary, and Psalms 75 and 76 answered with God's judgment and victory. Psalm 77 returns to the inner struggle of a person who can't see God at work. Its closing verses about the exodus lead directly into Psalm 78, the long historical psalm that retells Israel's story from Egypt to David. Psalm 77 ends at the Red Sea with Moses and Aaron; Psalm 78 takes up the story from there.
historical:
The heading reads “For the choirmaster. According to Jeduthun. A Psalm of Asaph.” Jeduthun was one of the three leaders of Levitical music appointed in David's day, alongside Asaph and Heman (1 Chronicles 16:41-42; 25:1-6). His name also appears in the headings of Psalms 39 and 62. According to Jeduthun may mean the psalm was to be performed by his guild of singers or in a style associated with him. For Asaph, see Psalm 73.

The psalm doesn't name the crisis behind it. The speaker's distress seems to be both personal and communal: he speaks as an individual but asks whether the Lord will spurn us forever (verse 7). Some scholars place it after the fall of the northern kingdom in 722 BC, since verse 15 mentions the sons of Jacob and Joseph (Joseph being the ancestor of the northern tribes Ephraim and Manasseh); others place it during or after the Babylonian exile, when the question of whether God had abandoned his people was acute. Still others treat it as a timeless lament. The poetic description of the sea crossing in verses 16 to 19 closely resembles the theophany (a dramatic appearance of God) in Habakkuk 3:10-15, and scholars debate which text draws on the other or whether both use a shared tradition.
cultural:
Night in the ancient world was a time of vulnerability and often of anxious thought. The speaker's outstretched hands (verse 2) describe the common posture of prayer, arms lifted toward heaven. His song in the night (verse 6) may refer to songs he once sang in happier times, now remembered with pain. The right hand of the Most High (verse 10) was a picture of God's power and favor in action; the speaker fears it has changed or grown weak.

The exodus was the defining story of Israel's identity, retold at Passover every year. The storm imagery in verses 17 and 18 (clouds, thunder, lightning as God's arrows, a whirlwind) echoes descriptions of God's appearing in power found in Exodus 19 and in many ancient Near Eastern texts about storm gods. The psalm uses the imagery to say that the LORD commanded the sea and sky as he led his people through the waters.
literary: The psalm divides into two halves that turn on verses 10 and 11. In verses 1 to 9 the pronouns are mostly I and my; the speaker is absorbed in his own distress, and his questions in verses 7 to 9 pile up in a series of six. In verses 11 to 20 the pronouns shift to You and Your; the speaker addresses God and recounts his deeds. The pivot is the word remember (zakar). In verse 3 remembering God only brings groaning, but in verse 11 remembering the works of the LORD changes the direction of the prayer. Verses 16 to 19 shift into a hymn in a different rhythm, with lines of three parallel phrases. The psalm ends quietly, with a shepherd image rather than a resolution of the speaker's feelings.

outline.t: Crying out to God in the day of trouble
Sleepless nights, remembering days of old
Leading his people like a flock

doctrines.note: The psalm voices the fear that God's love has ended and his promises have failed. It doesn't rush to an answer; the speaker's soul refuses comfort for a time, and Scripture includes that struggle as part of faith.
Verse 19 says God's way went through the sea, but his footprints could not be seen. God's guidance is real even when his hand is invisible, and his people may only see it looking back.
The exodus is the Old Testament's great picture of redemption: God redeeming his people by his power (verse 15) and leading them out of slavery. Remembering it sustains faith in present trouble.

words.note: Zakar, to remember. It appears in verses 3, 6, and 11. At first memory deepens the speaker's pain, since the past only highlights present loss. But in verse 11 he chooses to remember God's works, and memory becomes the path to hope.

Chesed, loving devotion or steadfast love. God's covenant loyalty is the heart of the speaker's question in verse 8: has it ended forever? The rest of the psalm answers by recalling the act that proved it, the exodus.

Pele, wonder or marvel. It describes acts beyond human power that reveal God, especially the wonders of the exodus. The speaker remembers God's wonders of old (verse 11) and confesses him as the God who works wonders (verse 14).

Aqev, heel or footprint. In verse 19 God's footprints were not to be found, since his path went through the sea itself. It is a striking picture of divine guidance that leaves no visible trace yet brings his people through.

christ: Psalm 77 isn't quoted in the New Testament, and its link to Jesus is thematic. Jesus himself prayed through the night (Luke 6:12) and in Gethsemane knew anguish that sought God and found no quick relief. The psalm's pivot, from asking whether God has forgotten to remembering how he redeemed his people, is the pattern the New Testament applies to the cross and resurrection: the greatest act of redemption becomes the event believers remember to sustain their hope (1 Corinthians 11:24-26). Jesus is also the good shepherd who leads his flock (John 10:11), fulfilling the psalm's closing image of God leading his people like sheep. And in walking on the sea and calming the storm, he displayed the same mastery over the waters that the psalm attributes to God (Mark 4:39-41; 6:48-51).
questions: When have you been unable to find comfort, even in prayer? What helped you through that time, if anything?
The speaker's turning point is a decision to remember God's works. What acts of God, in Scripture or your own life, do you return to when faith is hard?
Verse 19 says God's footprints were not seen. Where have you seen God's guidance only in hindsight?
